questions.q: Why does this lesson insist on running two separate evaluations rather than one?
options: Because a single evaluation metric is technically impossible to compute
Because a task-specific evaluation and a general-capability check answer different questions: whether the target behavior improved, and whether that improvement cost anything elsewhere (forgetting)
Because the lm-evaluation-harness requires exactly two tasks to run at all
Because two evaluations are always more statistically significant than one
questions.explain: Evaluating only the target task is exactly the blind spot the catastrophic forgetting lesson warned about. Running both a task-specific eval and a general-capability check reveals whether a task-metric win came with a hidden regression.

questions.q: What role does the held-out split from the dataset-building lesson play in this evaluation?
options: It is discarded once training completes and has no further use
It provides examples the model never trained on, used to measure genuine task-specific performance rather than performance on already-seen data
It is used only to compute the general-capability benchmark score
It replaces the need for comparing against the base model
questions.explain: The held-out split, set aside before training in the dataset-building lesson, is used here specifically because it was never seen during training, making the resulting task-specific score a genuine measure of generalization.

questions.q: What is the purpose of running the same general-capability benchmark subset (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K) against both the base model and the fine-tuned model?
options: To measure how much faster the fine-tuned model serves requests
To detect whether the fine-tune caused a regression in capabilities outside the fine-tuning task, i.e., catastrophic forgetting
To determine the exact license terms of the base model
To decide which quantization method to use for serving
questions.explain: Running the identical general-capability benchmark on both checkpoints isolates whether fine-tuning degraded capabilities outside the target task -- the same forgetting check introduced in the SFT chapter, now applied for real.

questions.q: How should a fine-tune that improves the task metric but causes a meaningful general-capability regression be treated, according to this lesson?
options: It should be discarded entirely and never reported, since any regression means total failure
It should be reported honestly as a trade-off -- a valid result to reason about, not a failure to hide
The regression should be omitted from the write-up since the task metric improved
It should be reported as an unambiguous success regardless of the regression's size
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states that a fine-tune winning on the task metric while regressing meaningfully elsewhere is still a result worth reporting honestly as a deliberate trade-off, not something to hide or treat as outright failure.

questions.q: In the PeftModel-based evaluation code shown, what does PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, adapter_path) accomplish?
options: It permanently merges the adapter weights into the base model's weights on disk
It wraps the loaded base model with the saved LoRA adapter so the combined model's behavior reflects the fine-tuning, without modifying the base weights
It deletes the base model and replaces it with a newly initialized model
It converts the model to a fully quantized GGUF format for llama.cpp
questions.explain: PeftModel.from_pretrained attaches the saved adapter weights to the base model at load time, producing the fine-tuned model's behavior for evaluation while the underlying base weights remain unchanged.
